translation: Chapter 1 Introduction
1.1 Motivation and Significance

Communication between the central nervous system and skeletal muscles occurs through electrical signals. Recording these signals at the skin surface produces surface electromyography, or sEMG. Because sEMG is directly related to muscular activity, it is one of the most important sources of information for the design of human–machine interfaces, intelligent prostheses, and rehabilitation systems.

The high noise level, stochastic nature, and strong dependence of sEMG signals on anatomical and physiological differences between individuals create significant challenges for signal processing and the extraction of precise motion information. Many existing systems recognize motion by performing discrete classification among a limited set of predefined movements. However, natural human hand motion is continuous, and joint angles change smoothly and gradually. This discrepancy between the discrete outputs of conventional models and the continuous nature of actual motion creates a need for models that can continuously estimate joint motion angles in real time.
1.2 Problem Definition

The principal objective of this project is to design and train a deep learning model that receives sEMG signals recorded from the forearm muscles and continuously and simultaneously estimates three wrist degrees of freedom: inward and outward rotation (Roll), upward and downward flexion (Pitch), and leftward and rightward deviation (Yaw). Unlike conventional approaches that classify discrete movements, this study seeks to provide continuous angular values within the normalized range from −1 to +1 for all three motion axes, allowing the model output to be used in systems for real-time control of hand prostheses or human–machine interfaces.
1.3 Related Research

Numerous studies have examined the extraction of motion information from sEMG signals. By introducing and comprehensively characterizing the NinaPro database, Atzori et al. established a standard reference for evaluating machine learning methods based on the simultaneous recording of muscle signals and hand kinematic data [1]. Subsequently, Gijsberts et al. introduced the movement error rate metric and extensively compared the performance of several machine learning methods on the same database [2]. Bao et al. proposed a hybrid CNN-LSTM architecture for estimating wrist kinematics from sEMG signals. In their framework, a convolutional network extracts deep features from the signal spectrum, after which an LSTM network processes these features for sequential regression [3]. In a related study, Quivira et al. used recurrent neural networks to translate sEMG signals into continuous hand poses [4].

In research closely related to this project, Du et al. proposed a hybrid TCN-LSTM model based on dilated convolutions for continuously estimating wrist joint angles from sEMG signals [5]. Ameri et al. also demonstrated improvements in simultaneous and proportional EMG control by proposing a regression convolutional neural network [6]. Finally, Atzori et al. applied deep convolutional neural networks to the NinaPro database and evaluated their ability to classify hand movements for intelligent prostheses [7]. Despite this substantial body of research, generalization across individuals remains an open challenge in this field. This issue was also investigated experimentally during the intermediate phases of the present project.
1.4 Project Contributions
The main contributions of this project are as follows:
A transition from discrete movement classification to continuous estimation of three wrist angles through label smoothing using a Gaussian low-pass filter.
Experimental investigation and practical demonstration of covariate shift in sEMG signals across individuals by comparing the Leave-One-Subject-Out and Global Repetition Split validation protocols.
Design of a hybrid CNN-LSTM architecture with dilated convolutions to expand the network's temporal receptive field without increasing the computational burden.
Introduction of a gain calibration technique to compensate for the conservative behavior induced by the MSE loss function and to bring the prediction amplitude closer to the actual movement values.
1.5 Report Organization

The remainder of this report is organized into four additional chapters. Chapter 2 presents the theoretical foundations of sEMG signals and wrist kinematics, together with a comprehensive introduction to the NinaPro DB2 database. Chapter 3 describes the complete development of the model through four research phases. Chapter 4 presents and analyzes the quantitative and qualitative results of the final model. Finally, Chapter 5 provides the conclusions, discusses the limitations, and proposes directions for future research.
Chapter 2 Theoretical Foundations and the Database
2.1 Surface Electromyography Signals

Surface electromyography records the electrical activity of muscles at the skin surface. Because these signals are nonstationary and contain motion and electrical noise, careful preprocessing is required before feature extraction. In this project, a Butterworth low-pass filter with a cutoff frequency of 5 Hz was combined with signal rectification using the absolute value to extract the signal's energy envelope.
2.2 Wrist Kinematics

The human wrist has three principal degrees of freedom. The Roll axis represents inward and outward rotation of the forearm. The Pitch axis represents upward and downward wrist flexion. The Yaw axis represents leftward and rightward wrist deviation. The objective of this project is to estimate all three angles continuously and simultaneously from sEMG signals.
Figure 2.1 Three wrist degrees of freedom: rotation (Roll), flexion (Pitch), and deviation (Yaw)
2.3 Introduction to the NinaPro DB2 Database

The standard NinaPro DB2 database was used to train and evaluate the deep learning models in this study. The NinaPro project was developed to provide a comprehensive reference collection of surface electromyography signals and hand kinematic data for advancing research on intelligent prostheses and human–machine interfaces. The DB2 subset specifically focuses on able-bodied individuals and is one of the richest available datasets in terms of movement diversity and equipment precision.
2.3.1 Participants

The DB2 database was collected from 40 able-bodied participants, including 28 men and 12 women, with a mean age of 29.9 years. All participants were right-handed and had no history of neurological or muscular disease. For model evaluation in this study, a subset of seven subjects, numbered 1, 7, 8, 11, 22, 25, and 35, was selected and processed because their recordings exhibited the highest signal quality and the lowest levels of motion noise.
2.3.2 Data Acquisition Equipment

The database acquisition system comprises two main components for measuring muscular activity and physical movement. The Delsys Trigno EMG acquisition system recorded muscle electrical activity using 12 wireless electrodes at a sampling frequency of 2,000 Hz. Eight electrodes were placed at equal intervals in a ring around the upper forearm, two electrodes were positioned over the principal flexor and extensor muscles, and two additional electrodes were placed over the biceps and triceps to record compound hand contractions. Simultaneously, a Cyberglove II kinematic acquisition system equipped with 22 sensors continuously recorded precise finger and wrist joint angles, enabling their use as regression labels when required.

2.3.3 Movement Protocol and Experimental Procedure

The experimental protocol was designed to minimize muscular fatigue while providing sufficient data for machine learning. Participants were instructed to sit in front of a monitor and imitate movements demonstrated in a video animation. Each specified movement was repeated exactly six times. During each repetition, the participant performed and maintained the movement for five seconds and then returned to a resting state for three seconds to prevent muscular fatigue.
2.3.4 Movement Categories

The DB2 dataset contains 50 different hand and wrist movements divided into three principal categories. Category A contains 17 basic, isolated finger and wrist movements. Category B contains 23 more complex movements, grasping patterns, and activities of daily living. Category C contains nine force application and object grasping patterns.

2.3.5 Alignment of the Data with the Research Objectives

Because the objective of this study was to continuously estimate three wrist motions, only movements associated with the Roll, Pitch, and Yaw degrees of freedom were filtered and extracted from the 50 available movements. In addition, postprocessing techniques and biomechanical filters, including Gaussian filtering of the labels, were used to convert the database's discrete, visually defined labels into continuous and natural motion trajectories, enabling regression models to support real-time control.
Chapter 3 Research Methodology and Model Development

The model was developed progressively through four consecutive research phases. In each phase, the results and limitations observed in the preceding phase informed a scientific decision to modify the architecture, the data, or the validation strategy. Each phase is described in detail in the following sections.
3.1 Phase 1 Development of the Baseline Intra Subject Model

The objective of this phase was to construct a baseline architecture that was robust to sEMG signal noise and prevented data leakage. An intra-subject training approach was adopted: the model was trained on repetitions 1, 3, 4, and 6 from subject 1 and evaluated on repetitions 2 and 5 from the same subject.
Figure 3.1 Baseline model development pipeline in Phase 1 under the intra-subject protocol
3.1.1 Development of Data Preprocessing

In the first version of this phase, the raw signal was used without amplitude filtering, and time windows were labeled using the mean label value within each window. This produced fractional labels at movement boundaries and confused the network when identifying the exact onset of motion. Two fundamental changes were introduced in the second version. First, the absolute signal value was used for rectification so that the signal's energy amplitude would be more interpretable to the network. Second, StandardScaler normalization was fitted exclusively to the training data and then applied to the test data to prevent data leakage. In addition, each window's label was changed to the label of its final sample so that prediction respected the principle of causality. In the fourth version, the time window was increased from 400 to 600 samples, corresponding to 300 milliseconds at a sampling frequency of 2,000 Hz. This allowed the network to observe a longer temporal context of muscular contraction before making a prediction.
3.1.2 Development of the Neural Network Architecture and Loss Functions

The model architecture began as a simple combination of one-dimensional convolution and a unidirectional LSTM with a mean squared error loss function. Because the labels were stepwise in this phase, the network exhibited substantial oscillations at movement boundaries. Consequently, the second version replaced the loss function with Huber loss, which combines linear and quadratic error terms and is more robust to abrupt changes. In the third version, conventional Dropout layers were replaced with SpatialDropout1D. Rather than disabling randomly selected neurons, this layer disables an entire feature map and is more effective for correlated EMG channel signals. The unidirectional LSTM was also upgraded to a bidirectional LSTM so that the network could analyze signal patterns in both the forward and backward directions within a window. In the fourth version, once the architecture had stabilized, the number of training epochs was increased from 25 to 60. The model then reduced the validation error to an acceptable level without severe overfitting.
3.1.3 Key Decisions in This Phase

Two fundamental decisions brought the results closer to the standards reported in established research publications. First, the intra-subject protocol replaced the pooling of data from multiple individuals to avoid the substantial loss of accuracy caused by covariate shift. Second, from the middle of this phase onward, a moving-average filter with a specified window length was applied to the predicted outputs. This considerably smoothed the output curve and made it suitable for more precise motion recognition.
3.1.4 Achievements and Limitations of Phase 1

This phase established a robust baseline architecture and addressed data leakage, resulting in stable model outputs for a single individual. However, the fundamental limitation was that the model remained restricted to data from one particular user. This limitation motivated Phase 2, which investigated whether the architecture could be extended by pooling data from multiple users to obtain a more general model.
Figure 3.2 Performance of the Phase 1 baseline model on the test data of a single subject
3.2 Phase 2 Evaluation of the Generalized Inter Subject Model

In this phase, the research approach shifted from a single individual toward the development of a general model. The main objective was to pool data from multiple users and train a network capable of correctly recognizing movement patterns despite anatomical and physiological differences between individuals.
3.2.1 Pooling and Integration of Multiple Datasets

Data from seven different subjects were processed to construct a comprehensive model. At this stage, each subject's training and test data were separately extracted, filtered, and rectified, and were subsequently combined using array concatenation. Data were segmented into windows of 600 samples with a step of 50 samples. This produced a global training matrix containing more than 107,000 time windows and a test matrix containing approximately 52,000 windows.
3.2.2 Architectural Development for Complex Data

The substantial increase in diversity within the pooled data required a major architectural upgrade. The first version used a simpler structure consisting of one-dimensional convolution layers, max pooling, conventional Dropout layers with a rate of 0.2, and a unidirectional LSTM. This architecture contained 134,291 trainable parameters and had difficulty identifying stable patterns across the diverse signals of different individuals. In the second version, the conventional Dropout layers were replaced with SpatialDropout1D. The most important change was the upgrade of the recurrent layer to a bidirectional LSTM, which improved the model's ability to understand the signal's temporal sequence in both directions. These modifications increased the number of network parameters to more than 238,000.

3.2.3 Learning Rate Control Strategy

As the network grew and the loss landscape became more complex, EarlyStopping with a patience of 15 epochs was used to prevent overfitting. ReduceLROnPlateau was also used to reduce the initial learning rate of 0.001 by a factor of 0.5 when the validation error stopped decreasing. This produced smoother convergence during the final training epochs.
3.2.4 Achievements and Limitations of Phase 2

This phase produced a deeper network capable of processing the large volume of data from seven users without interruption or severe overfitting. Nevertheless, the principal weakness at this stage was the network's inability to fully capture long-term signal dependencies amid this high level of diversity, which reduced prediction accuracy. This challenge motivated Phase 3, in which dilated convolutions were introduced to expand the network's receptive field and inter-subject validation strategies were evaluated in greater detail.

3.3 Phase 3 Improvements to the Spatiotemporal Architecture and Validation Strategies
Phase 3 focused on expanding the network's receptive field and examining different cross-validation protocols to address inter-subject differences.
3.3.1 Data Partitioning Strategies

Under the Leave-One-Subject-Out protocol, the network was trained on six subjects, while one subject was held out entirely for testing. Because the model encountered completely new anatomy, fine-tuning and transfer learning were implemented, with only the final dense layers trained using a limited amount of data from the new subject. Under the Global Repetition Split protocol, repetitions 1, 3, 4, and 6 from all seven subjects were used for training, and repetitions 2 and 5 from all subjects were used for testing. This allowed the model to become familiar with the signal diversity of all individuals simultaneously.
3.3.2 Architectural Improvements Using Dilated Convolutions

The dilation rate was introduced into the architecture to enable the network to capture a longer period of muscular contraction. Three convolution layers with increasing dilation rates of 1, 2, and 4 were used in this phase, allowing the network to extract high-frequency features and the overall movement trend simultaneously. GlobalAveragePooling1D was also used in the aggregation stage to increase the model's robustness to temporal shifts in the signal.
Figure 3.4 Dilated convolutions and expansion of the network's receptive field
3.3.3 Advanced Kinematic Postprocessing

A Savitzky–Golay filter replaced the simple moving-average filter. This filter removed high-frequency noise from the neural network's prediction curve without eliminating the peaks required for movement recognition.
3.3.4 Achievements and the Fundamental Challenge of Phase 3

In Phase 3, the network architecture reached its highest level of maturity in feature extraction. However, analysis of the results revealed a fundamental scientific challenge: regardless of the extent of training on pooled samples from multiple subjects, recognition performance remained very low for a completely new individual. Covariate shift in sEMG signals across individuals was so substantial that constructing a fully general model appeared practically impossible, even when transfer learning was applied to the final layers. This generalization impasse redirected the overall project strategy toward a subject-specific approach in Phase 4, this time with the objective of fully continuous recognition rather than discrete classification.

Figure 3.6 Output of the Phase 3 model under the Global Repetition Split protocol
3.4 Phase 4 Transition to Continuous Kinematics and Final Calibration

The shift to intra-subject training to overcome users' physiological differences transformed the project from a simple discrete classification problem into a continuous estimation system. Because a human hand cannot change its angle instantaneously in a stepwise manner, fitting the sharp edges of the original labels produced oscillations. Two innovations introduced in this phase addressed this problem.
3.4.1 Smoothing the Target Labels

At this stage, the previous label-generation function was replaced with a new function that applied a Gaussian low-pass filter with a sigma of 400 to the stepwise labels. This innovation caused the network's targets to simulate natural muscular behavior, including gradual acceleration, reaching a peak, and smooth deceleration to a stop. Rather than memorizing discontinuities, the neural network identified a coherent, continuous motion trajectory for all three angles.
Figure 3.7 Smoothing discrete stepwise labels into continuous kinematic trajectories using a Gaussian low-pass filter
3.4.2 Initial Evaluation and Amplitude Attenuation

Applying the model to the smoothed targets produced substantial improvements in temporal alignment, and the Pearson correlation coefficients for the motion axes reached high values. However, the use of the MSE loss function and weight penalties induced conservative behavior: at the peaks of movement, the model stopped at lower amplitudes instead of reaching the absolute target values.
3.4.3 Gain Calibration and Output Clipping

Gain calibration was used to address the failure to reach movement peaks without disrupting temporal correlation. To match the prediction amplitude to the actual movement amplitude, a gain factor of 1.35 was applied to the model output, and the resulting values were clipped to the permitted range from −1 to +1. When clipping limited the prediction, this technique produced a flat plateau at the peaks of the curve, ensuring stable motion recognition at the extreme angles.
Figure 3.8 Effect of gain calibration on compensating for attenuation of the model's output amplitude
3.4.4 Final Model Architecture

The final model combines CNN and LSTM layers because a standalone CNN does not capture the movement sequence, whereas a standalone LSTM is computationally demanding and performs poorly when extracting features from highly fluctuating raw signals. The model layers are arranged as follows:
Addition of random Gaussian noise at the input to improve robustness to sensor noise under real-world conditions.
Two Conv1D layers with L2 regularization to extract high-frequency spatial features.
BatchNormalization and MaxPooling layers to accelerate convergence and reduce dimensionality.
A SpatialDropout1D layer with a rate of 0.2 to prevent overfitting in spatial feature maps.
An LSTM layer with 64 units to extract complex, long-term temporal dependencies.
A GlobalAveragePooling1D layer for robust feature aggregation.
An output Dense layer mapping 64 features to 3 outputs for simultaneous linear regression of the three motion axes.
Figure 3.9 Detailed architecture of the final hybrid CNN-LSTM neural network

Taken together, the four phases represent a scientific development process. The project began with an initial architecture using discrete labels, demonstrated and confronted the difficulties of constructing a general model for new subjects, and ultimately returned to an optimized intra-subject approach. By incorporating biomechanical principles and calibration, it produced a practical and accurate model for continuous and simultaneous recognition of three hand motions.

As shown in Table 4.1, the highest accuracy was obtained for the Pitch axis, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9634, indicating that more than 96 percent of this axis's angular behavior was correctly predicted by the model. The Roll and Yaw axes also yielded acceptable results, with correlation coefficients of 0.8707 and 0.8949, respectively.
4.2 Visual Analysis of the Results

Visual inspection of the final model's output on the test data shows that the prediction curves for all three axes agree closely with the actual angles, without the substantial oscillations and high-frequency noise observed in Phases 2 and 3. Label smoothing enabled the network to capture the natural slope of muscular movement. Gain calibration allowed the predictions to settle stably at the maximum angles, without oscillation, within the range from −1 to +1. The limited residual noise at some points is likely attributable to hand tremor during dataset acquisition rather than a weakness of the model.

4.3 Discussion

The results of this project support two important scientific findings. First, the hybrid CNN-LSTM architecture with dilated convolutions is effective for jointly extracting spatial features and long-term temporal dependencies from sEMG signals. Second, covariate shift in biological signals across individuals is a real phenomenon that substantially limits general inter-subject training without advanced transfer learning techniques. Consequently, a subject-specific intra-subject training approach is the more reasonable choice for achieving the highest possible accuracy with the current technology.
Chapter 5 Conclusions
5.1 Overview of the Findings

This project designed and developed a deep learning model for continuously and simultaneously estimating three wrist motion axes, namely Roll, Pitch, and Yaw, from sEMG signals. Development proceeded through four progressive phases, in which the network evolved from a simple intra-subject model to a general inter-subject model and finally to an advanced intra-subject model with continuous outputs. The principal achievements include addressing data leakage in Phase 1, experimentally demonstrating covariate shift in Phase 3, and introducing two key innovations in Phase 4: Gaussian label smoothing and gain calibration. On the test data, the final model achieved a Pearson correlation coefficient above 0.87 on all three motion axes, which the study considers a reliable value for practical implementation.
Figure 5.1 Overview of the project's development through four phases
5.2 Limitations
Because the final model uses intra-subject training, it cannot be applied directly to new individuals without calibration or readjustment.
Covariate shift in sEMG signals across individuals remains unresolved, and the methods used in this project did not enable the construction of a fully general model.
The final evaluation was based on laboratory data from the NinaPro DB2 database. Model performance in real-world and noisier operating conditions has not yet been examined.
5.3 Recommendations for Future Research
Investigate more advanced transfer learning and domain adaptation methods to reduce the effects of covariate shift across individuals.
Implement the model on embedded hardware with limited computational resources for use in portable intelligent prostheses.
Collect a dedicated dataset from a larger number of users under more varied acquisition conditions to evaluate model generalization more thoroughly.
Investigate Transformer-based architectures for modeling long-term temporal dependencies in sEMG signals.
